title: IEA Oil Market Report (October 2026)
source: EST: the IEA's standing monthly mid-month cadence, established against its own primary PDFs — iea.blob.core.windows.net filenames encode release dates and four were re-verified HTTP 200 on 2026-09-15 (-21JAN2026, -12MAR2026, -14APR2026, -13MAY2026 _OilMarketReport*.pdf) — plus the September 2026 edition's own observed release on 2026-09-11, corroborated by four independent same-day trade-press reads. THE DATE ITSELF WAS NOT READ ON ANY PAGE THIS SESSION COULD FETCH, AND IS LABELLED ACCORDINGLY: a search-index read returned 14 October 2026 (and 13 November 2026 after it), but investing.com's IEA calendar page returned HTTP 403 to curl with a browser UA and, fetched through a converting reader, had not rolled forward — it still listed Sep 11 as the next release, with history rows Dec 11 2025 through Aug 12 2026. iea.org returned HTTP 403 on /reports, /topics/oil-market-report and /events to both curl and a converting fetcher, the third consecutive session it has done so. STAYS ESTIMATE on four counts: the primary schedule page is unreadable, the aggregator table is stale, the source-prefix taxonomy defines no IEA: confirmed prefix, and the event-research lane may not self-confirm an event it discovered in-sweep. Release time is the IEA's standing 10:00 Paris = 04:00 ET. Proposed 2026-09-15
notes: Proposed by the iea-omr-2026-09-11 close-out, which its own initial research had left explicitly undated ('next OMR mid-October 2026 (undated here) - the IEA schedule page 403s'). Filed low on the same reasoning as its September sibling, eia-steo-2026-09-09 and opec-momr-2026-09-10: a forecast publication sets no policy and moves no equity tape, and it lands 5.5 hours before the US equity open where USO and XLE have zero hourly bars across a full two-year sample. WHOEVER RESEARCHES THIS MUST RE-DERIVE THE DATE FIRST - it is a cadence estimate, not a read. Two live questions this edition is the next test of, both from the September close-out. (1) The IEA-minus-EIA Gulf shut-in offset looked like a definitional constant near 3.35 mb/d rather than a live disagreement - August 10.1 vs 6.72, July 8.3 vs 4.98, against baselines 6.8 mb/d apart (IEA implied pre-war 32.0, EIA Feb-26 25.2). Proved wrong by this edition and the October STEO differing by more than +/-0.7 mb/d from 3.35 on the September month, or by either agency restating its baseline. (2) The release-window base rate needs a clean session: the 2026-09-11 window was the largest release-hour move in 13 observations on both crude benchmarks (CL=F -1.168%, BZ=F -1.540%), but three own-hour p95 outliers preceded the report by 3-8 hours, so it scored unscoreable rather than a kill. A release-window forward test registered for this edition should pre-register its control - the session's other hours against their own-hour distribution, plus a placebo instrument - instead of a threshold with a prose attribution clause.
